<h1 align="center">Unmasking the Data</h1>

<p align="center"> Exploring Data with R </p>

<p align="center"> Unmask your data with simple data manipulation functions and a custom plotting theme! </p>

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->


## Overview

The unmasked package provides a way to make data exploration, summarization, and visualization easier and more approachable. By combining workflow moves and functions to calculate group percentages and organize the data, unmasked helps to uncover patterns in the data and clearly communicate the findings.

Whether you're exploring a new data set, completing a class assignment, or creating a polished visualization, unmasked offers you the opportunity to do more with your data.

## Why use unmasked?

Summarizing observations, calculating percentages, and formatting plots often become a repetitive and time consuming process. With unmasked, this process is made much simpler by bringing together helpful functions and a custom theme.

- **Simplify data exploration**: Work with a data set using simple data moves to manipulate and explore the data.
- **Calculate group percentages**: Use the helper function `percent_by_group()` to examine how much each group contributes to the total.
- **Create clean visualizations**: Use the theme function `theme_trap()` to organize the data and create consistent and pleasing visualizations with a soft pastel color palette.
- **Make findings easier to communicate**: Combine the data summaries and visualizations to professionally present your findings of the data.

## Installation

You can install the development version of unmasked from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("icl003/unmasked")
```
Load the package with: `library(unmasked)`

## Main Functions

### percent_by_group()

The `percent_by_group()` function calculates the number of observations in each category of a specific variable and gives the percentage of the total that this number represents. This is useful for quickly understanding the distribution of a categorical variable with out having to write out all of the calculations.

For example, using the scoobydoo data set from Tidy Tuesday:

```{r helper}
library(tidytuesdayR)
library(unmasked)

tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2021, week = 29)
scoobydoo <- tuesdata$scoobydoo

percent_by_group(scoobydoo, network)
```

We used the function to provide both the count and percentage for each network, which allows us to explore how episodes are distributed across different networks.

### theme_trap()

The `theme_trap()` function provides a theme with a simple, clean, consistent layout, with a soft pastel-like aesthetic. It focuses on blues, using navy for text, a lighter blue for graph lines and highlights, as well as a complementary light peach background to tie the graph together. These colors come from the brand, which uses a similar color palette focused on blues but also includes peaches and browns which all tie together nicely.

For example, using the scoobydoo data set from Tidy Tuesday:

```{r theme}
library(tidytuesdayR)
library(unmasked)
library(ggplot2)

tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2021, week = 29)
scoobydoo <- tuesdata$scoobydoo

ggplot(scoobydoo, aes(x = format, fill = format)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "#3A405A",
      "#E9A4A3",
      "#99B2DD",
      "#C98F7A",
      "#F9DEC9"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Scooby-Doo Media Format Used",
    subtitle = "Number of episodes by media format",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of Episodes",
    caption = "Source: tidy tuesday scoobydoo dataset"
  ) +
  theme_trap()
```

Applying the theme function gives a consistent and clean visual layout that avoids non-data-ink without all the additional manual coding.

#### The brand

I wanted to closely tie together my brand and the theme function I chose to create. The brand I created first, spending way too long deciding on a color palette. I've always loved blue, so the main color of the brand and the theme are blue, darker blues for the text, and light blues for some accent colors. I went through many complementary color options, finding that peaches, creams, and browns looked quite nice. I used the majority of these as accent colors, especially the lighter color options as they'd be hard to read if used as the color for small font. The fonts are both a simple, clean looking serif font, which I then utilized more within the theme as axis labels and sub headers and captions. For my brand, I chose to link my LinkedIn, since this is such an emerging field and place to find work and connect with people.

## Exploring the Scooby-Doo dataset

The unmasked package can be used with dplyr to investigate different datasets. Here, we used the scoobydoo data set to look at examples. Using this dataset, you can explore questions such as:

- Which episodes feature real monsters?
- How many episodes fall into each monster category?
- Which episodes have the longest run times?
- How are episodes distributed across networks and media formats?

For example, with the scoobydoo data set from Tidy Tuesday, you can filter the episodes featuring real monsters:

```{r filter}
library(dplyr)

scooby_filtered <- scoobydoo %>%
  filter(monster_real == TRUE)
```

Where we now have a filtered data set that only includes episodes where the monster was identified as real.

We can also group episodes by whether or not the monster was real, and provide a summary count of the episodes in each group.

```{r group}
library(dplyr)

scooby_groupby <- scoobydoo %>%
  group_by(monster_real) %>%
  summarize(episode_count = n())
```

These examples portray how the unmasked package fits into a larger data workflow, and is able to complement simple data move dplyr functions with convenient summary and visualization tools.

## Dependencies

The examples in this README use these R packages:

- `dplyr` for data manipulation
- `ggplot2` for visualizations
- `tidytuesdayR` to access the scoobydoo dataset used in the examples

You can install these with:

`install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "tidytuesdayR"))`
